newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Britain's Clarke plays down EMU investment fear.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke plays down EMU investment fear.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Friday played down concerns that London's wait-and-see stance on monetary union could hit foreign investment.

Reacting to a warning by the chairman of Japanese car giant Toyota, Haoroshi Okuda, that his company could opt to build factories in continental Europe instead, Clarke said that he was certain investors understood that whatever decision Britain took would be in the country's interests.

"The government's position is very reassuring to all those Japanese investors who have committed themselves to the British economy and Japanese investors who I hope will continue to do so," he told a news conference at the World Economic Forum.

Okuda stirred up a political storm with his warning on Wednesday that the company could lose interest in Britain if it stayed out of European Union plans to launch a single currency -- the euro -- in January 1999.

The official British position is that it has not yet made up its mind but the government of Prime Minister John Major is under fierce political pressure from the Eurosceptic wing of the Conservative party to make a commitment to stay out.
Clarke, who makes no secret of his sympathy for the single currency idea, reaffirmed that the government was determined to keep its options open on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
On a recent visit to Tokyo he had spelled out Britain's position on Europe to leading Japanese investors and they had been perfectly happy with the position it, Clarke said.
"I found that all the Japanese businessmen that I addressed did not challenge or query that policy. They were immensely reassured by it."

"I think they understand the caution, keeping one's options open. They look at our economic record and they trust our judgement to preserve for them the best base for manufacturing investment in western Europe," he said.
Earlier, Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies dismissed suggestions that uncertainty over Britain's membership of EMU could weaken London as a financial centre.
"So far, the uncertainty about EMU has not had any serious effect on the City of London," he told journalists in Davos.

Clarke reaffirmed his view that European states would probably not meet the January 1999 launch date for EMU because not enough countries would be in a position to satisfy its stiff economic entry tests.
In fact, one of the key factors determining Britain's eventual decision would be the extent to which member countries' economies had genuinely converged, he said.
Although the European Union could miss the start date, the political momentum in favour of monetary union was so strong that the launch might not be long delayed, he added.
